seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Copper Stair Paper

blocks.text: Lisle said yes to every line. Then she held out her hand for the pen and said, 'Give it here, I'll initial the lot so you can't move me to f—'
She stopped.
Her mouth stayed open on the word. Her fingers stayed curled for the pen, an inch above the Stall Book. She did not blink.

I had just written all two hundred and five of her MD9 seconds into her sleep: half an hour at three in the morning on six nights, twenty-five minutes on the seventh. Her whole match had cost her under four hours of stall, and none of it was due now.
The Bank's spot-check clerk sat at the window with his pen lifted. He watched her. He did not write anything, and he did not say anything.

Coyle had lowered her hand in the last Bank minute without calling. The Arbiter had read the slates, thirty-four to thirty-three, and the Hour had ended at the stroke it began with. Nine to eight. Eleven points. Twenty minutes later we were in the porter's lodge at the foot of our tower for the Close, and Lisle had talked the whole way down the stairs.
Now she was not talking. On the bench by the door Drewe had stopped turning her screwdriver. Tran had woken up.
I watched Lisle's hand. The lodge clock said twenty-two minutes past twelve when she stopped. It said twenty-eight when her fingers closed on the pen.
'—our o'clock,' she said, and initialled the first line.
She had felt nothing. I could see that. She looked up for the laugh and found Drewe's face instead.
'You went,' Drewe said. 'Six minutes. Like a carriage clock with a bent pallet. Just sat there not ticking.'
Lisle looked at the lodge clock. She looked at it for longer than it takes to read a clock. Then she laughed and said, 'Two coppers says it's the cold in here.'
Nobody took the bet.
I wrote the six minutes on my own sheet, under the Stall Book, with the time. I did not ask her anything yet.

Her MD9 debt was in the book, every second of it, at three in the morning. Her MD8 stalls had all fallen as I wrote them. The MD7 Week of Grace had ended a week ago. A stall at twenty-two minutes past midnight, with no line of mine against it, came from somebody's issue, and it was not mine.
My verdict was plain. Lisle owed a debt I had never issued, and she knew it. She had looked at the clock before she laughed.

At the next table Hester Coyle was weighing Bellpull's jar. Her Tally had finished at fifty-six spent and two hundred and forty-four banked, so her jar should read two hundred and forty-four, all of it in the bank chamber. She read the dial, wrote, and capped her pen. Then she spoke without looking up.
'I tell every new Reckoner I'll call it,' she said. 'Nine years. I've never called one.'
I said nothing.
'You watched my hands for four rounds instead of your slates. That's what it's for.' She slid her jar across to her own clerk. 'And big early is just how I bank. Ask anyone.'
Drewe had told me that a week before. Drewe had been right, and I had not.
Behind me Tran said, 'Mm.'
'I thought you meant it,' I said to Coyle. 'I was wrong.'
She looked at me then, for the first time since the stroke. 'You played the back half well. Everyone's wrong about me once.' She buttoned her coat and went out.

I sent the others to wait on the steps. Lisle said the clerk would want to watch me sign my name and she wasn't missing that, and Drewe took her by the elbow and walked her out. Tran went last, carrying the chicory jug.
The Bank brought its own scale to my Closes now. The clerk set it on the ledge of the window. I checked the empty pan read zero. Then I set the jar on it, barehanded.
It read a hundred and twenty-five. The glass was still warm.
'Declaration,' the clerk said.

'Issue three hundred. Tally spent two hundred and ten, banked seventy-one. The jar should hold ninety. It holds a hundred and twenty-five. Thirty-five over, warm.' A total without its split is not a declaration, so I gave him the split. 'Five is friction on seconds I did not issue. The Tally counted it, and it never left the jar. Thirty were wound in and came back to the jar unspent.'

I knew what I was handing him. A surplus declared at the Close goes to the Bank, and within seven days the Bank rules it Pool Fraud or a calibration error. Pool Fraud forfeits the match after the fact. Nine to eight would become a loss, and eleven points would be eight again. A Reckoner who declares honestly is not personally penalised. Her side is.

The clerk did not write any of it down. He stamped the declaration, blotted it and put it in the Bank bag with the jar. He had not read it. He wrote the time in his book, twelve forty-one, and the Bank's seven days began.
After MD7 the Bank had found the porter's-lodge scale reading forty-seven high, and the result had stood. Tonight the scale was the Bank's own.
An argument would have told me what the Bank thought. The stamp told me nothing, and that worried me more.
On the steps Lisle asked whether I had signed my name nicely. I said I had. I did not tell any of them what I had declared.

I wanted two things that week. I wanted to know whose warm seconds Drewe's hands had been winding, and I wanted the Bank to let us keep the win. I could only work on the first. Each morning I looked for a Bank envelope on my desk at the Guild, and each morning there was none.

The next afternoon, before the filing, I started a variance column on the graph paper at the back of my notebook. MD7, forty-seven over, warm. MD8, nothing over, cold. MD9, thirty-five over, warm. The column was right. It did not tell me whose waiting the seconds had come from.
On the second afternoon I sat with Drewe on the bench by the Ninth Stair gate. Tran was asleep at the other end with his chin on his chest and the jug between his boots.
'Why did the mainspring hand in its notice?' Drewe said. 'It was sick of being w—'
She stopped. Her screwdriver was halfway through a turn between her fingers, and it stayed there. I looked at my watch.

I had issued Drewe nothing at MD9. I had booked nothing for her. Her MD8 stalls had all fallen as I wrote them, and the MD7 week was over. By the printed Laws there was one debt she could still owe from MD9: friction on seconds I had not issued, charged to the Winder whose hands moved them. The Tally had counted five. Five seconds of friction is five minutes of stall.
At five minutes the screwdriver finished its turn.
'—ound up,' Drewe said. She looked at my face and then at my watch. 'Did I go?'
'Five minutes.'
'Old paper,' she said. 'MD7. Bit of grit in the train.' She went back to turning the screwdriver, faster than before.
It was not MD7. I did not say so.
'May I see your gran's box?' I said.
She took it out of her coat and turned it over twice. Then she pressed the catch with her thumbnail and opened it. Nobody on the landing had seen inside it before, as far as I knew.
'Mind,' she said. 'She sneezes at strangers.'

It was empty. There was brown dust in the corners of the lid, and it smelled of old snuff. I held it in my bare palm. It was cold, as cold as the bench. I closed it and gave it back, and she put it away without looking at it.
My verdict was that it was a keepsake after all. Whatever brass Drewe's hands had wound those seconds from, it was not this box. Somebody else had the brass, and somebody else had filled it.

By the evening of the second day Lisle had stalled ten times that I knew of, counting the Close. Twice on the warehouse floor on the first morning, eight minutes and three. Her foreman wrote the first in his book and told her she was finished at the end of the week; his nephew would have her bench. He wrote the second as well. Nine minutes on the fourth stair of her lodging house, one hand on the rail; the landlady found her. On the second day, ten minutes in the chophouse with Tran, seven in the street, five on a tram with Drewe beside her, and three more she told me about herself. None of them was at three in the morning. Every one was between one minute and ten.
I went to her lodgings after the filing. She was sitting at the kitchen table with her chair pulled well back from the stove. The coal bucket was where it had been.
I put my sheet in front of her.
'Two hundred and five, booked into your sleep at three,' I said. 'Seventy-one minutes of stalls in two days that I know of. None of them at three. That isn't my issue.'
She put both hands flat on the table and looked at them. She did not make a bet.

'Felix Wardle,' she said. 'My Reckoner at the Copper Stair. He Deferred me. Everything I spent for two seasons, he rolled it on. Three in the hundred a week. He said why serve it now, when you'll be in the Belfry and can afford the time.' She turned one hand over. 'I knew it was banned. Everybody knows. I let him.'
'The letter,' I said.

'I fished it out of the bucket after you'd gone. Bank form. It said Felix had a week to sign his renewal, and if he didn't, the lot would fall due in the Week of Grace after my next match.' She looked up. 'He didn't sign. Five hundred and thirty-eight seconds.'
Five hundred and thirty-eight seconds is eight hours and fifty-eight minutes of stall. Less what had fallen, it would come in chunks of one to ten minutes, waking or asleep, for five more days.
'Why d'you think I wasn't betting?' she said. 'Before Bellpull.'
'I thought you were nervous about Bellpull,' I said. 'I was wrong.'
Illegal Deferral is a League offence. I knew how to report one. I did not.
My verdict I kept to myself. She had hidden crooked paper from the team since the day she came to the Ninth Stair. Someone who could hide that could hide other things.
'Book it,' she said. 'Put it at three. Put it anywhere.'
'I can't. Only the Reckoner who issued a debt can book it. Wardle issued it.'
'Then find Felix.'
'Nobody has seen him since the Copper Stair folded.'
She went very quiet. I could hear the landlady's clock in the hall. When she spoke again her voice was low and even, and I had not heard it like that before.
'Everything I spend from now on,' she said. 'You book it. All of it. I'll say yes to every line.'
She had said yes to every line at the Close. This was not the same. She was asking. I think it was the first time she understood what the book was for.
I took out her week map. Stairs, stoves, rails. She was not to be alone near any of them until the week was out. Tran and Drewe would have to know why.
'I'll tell them,' she said. 'Not you. Me.'
She told them that night on the landing, all of it, with her hands in her pockets. Drewe stopped turning the screwdriver. Tran listened with his eyes shut.
'Mm,' Tran said. 'I'll sleep on your floor. Sleeping's my best event.'
'I'll do mornings,' Drewe said. 'I'll be your escapement. Let you out one tick at a time.'
'Two coppers says I'm sick of the lot of you by day five,' Lisle said.
'Taken,' said Drewe.

I wrote it into the map. Tran on her floor at night. Drewe from her door to the Guild Hall stop each morning, to put her on the six-forty. Me on that tram already, off the night desk, to ride with her to the warehouse. The foreman put her on sweeping, away from the ladders, and wrote every stall in his book.

On the third day the cover held. Lisle stalled five times under it and none of them was near a stair. Drewe told me Lisle had complained twice about being walked like a dog and had held Drewe's sleeve both times they crossed a road.

I walked home past the Guild Hall after the filing. The clock over the tram stop outside it was two minutes behind my watch, which I set at the Regulator's stroke every night at the desk. Public clocks are the Guild's to keep. I wrote the stop and the two minutes in my notebook.

The queue under the clock was longer than the timetable explained. A man in a grey coat kept checking his watch against the clock, shaking his wrist and checking again. A woman with a string bag of potatoes moved it from her right hand to her left, and back, and back again. Nobody spoke. I walked on.
The next morning my tram was a minute late.

I saw the Guild Hall stop from the window as we came in. Drewe was walking away towards the corner. Lisle was alone on the kerb, with the other line's rails between her and my tram. She saw me at the window and stepped off the kerb.
On the rails she stopped, mid-stride, one hand lifted to push her hair back.

I was down the step before the tram had settled. I crossed to her. Her hand was still lifted, the fingers spread, a strand of hair caught over one knuckle. Her eyes were open and fixed on the window I had been sitting at.
I was afraid. I looked at her hand.
The timetable board under the clock gave the next tram on that line at six forty-one. The clock over it said six thirty-nine and a half. Yesterday it had been two minutes slow.
I took her arm in both hands and pulled, and she was rigid and as heavy as a statue, and I could not move her.
